impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder's conditioning of patent licenses on customers' exclusive purchase of unpatented products constitutes unlawful tying under the Sherman Act, and whether the tied products had substantial non-infringing uses that would preclude antitrust liability.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a jury verdict finding that Ingevity engaged in unlawful tying by conditioning licenses to its fuel vapor canister patent on customers' agreements to exclusively purchase Ingevity's unpatented carbon honeycomb products. The court upheld the antitrust liability and corresponding damages award, determining that the question of whether the tied products had substantial non-infringing uses was properly submitted to the jury.
impacts.positiveImplications: Competitors of dominant patent holders benefit from reinforced protections against leveraging patent rights to foreclose competition in adjacent unpatented product markets.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face significant antitrust liability risk if they condition patent licenses on exclusive purchasing arrangements for unpatented products, even where the products are related to the patented technology.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that pharmaceutical patent claims directed to methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents covering treatment methods using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies, after a jury had found willful infringement by Eli Lilly. The court's reversal reinstates a jury verdict of willful infringement in a high-stakes biologics patent dispute between major pharmaceutical companies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech patent holders benefit from a more favorable standard for written description and enablement, particularly for genus claims in the antibody space where prior art methods of making and humanizing antibodies were well-known.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face renewed patent enforcement risk in the antibody therapeutics space, as broader genus claims covering classes of biological molecules may survive validity challenges.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to methods for detecting anomalous program executions using emulators and models of function calls are directed to abstract ideas under step one of the Alice framework, and whether the district court erred in awarding damages based on foreign sales.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia University against Norton (Gen Digital), holding that the asserted cybersecurity patent claims are abstract at Alice step one and remanding for further proceedings on step two. The court also ruled that the district court erred in allowing damages based on Norton's foreign sales, significantly limiting the potential damages recovery.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies benefit from strengthened § 101 eligibility defenses against software-related patent claims, particularly those involving detection and comparison methods that the court found abstract.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting software and cybersecurity patents face heightened Alice eligibility risks, and the ruling on foreign sales damages limits the ability to recover royalties on worldwide product sales in U.S. patent cases.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether summary judgment was proper on claims of inequitable conduct in patent prosecution and Walker Process antitrust fraud based on the alleged concealment of prior art (the CYMAX Documents) during patent prosecution.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment on both inequitable conduct and Walker Process fraud claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to whether Tenaris committed fraud on the patent office by concealing prior art documents when obtaining coiled tubing patents. The case was remanded for trial on both the patent unenforceability and antitrust claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Competitors benefit from the court's willingness to allow Walker Process antitrust claims to proceed to trial where there is evidence of deliberate concealment of material prior art during patent prosecution.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face dual exposure to inequitable conduct and antitrust liability if they fail to disclose material prior art during prosecution, with potential for treble damages under the antitrust laws.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court properly granted summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality grounds where the accused multi-core processor selection method was performed partly outside the United States, and whether VLSI's doctrine of equivalents theory was properly rejected.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part Intel's summary judgment of noninfringement of VLSI's multicore processor patent, finding that genuine disputes of material fact remained regarding where the accused method steps were performed and whether doctrine of equivalents applied. The case involves claims about selecting processor cores based on performance parameters.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the court's rejection of broad extraterritoriality defenses, preserving infringement claims where accused processes may have domestic components even when products are manufactured globally.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies with global manufacturing and design operations face continued uncertainty about extraterritorial reach of U.S. method patents, particularly for semiconductor and processor technologies.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit issued a mixed ruling in a patent infringement case involving digital communication constellation designs, vacating eligibility for some claims while affirming for others, and affirming the jury's infringement and damages findings. The court distinguished between claims that recite specific technical implementations and those directed to abstract mathematical concepts.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations in communication standards may maintain eligibility even when the underlying technology involves mathematical optimization, providing a roadmap for drafting eligible claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing industry communication standards face ongoing patent exposure, and the split eligibility ruling creates uncertainty about which formulations of standards-related claims will survive § 101 challenges.

impacts.caseName: Apple Inc. v. International Trade Commission
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features infringed Masimo's patents for user-worn noninvasive physiological measurement devices, and whether Masimo established a domestic industry.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watches that infringed Masimo's wearable blood oxygen measurement patents, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation. The court found no error in the ITC's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the wearable health technology space benefit from the affirmation that ITC exclusion orders remain a powerful tool to block infringing imports of consumer electronics incorporating patented health-monitoring features.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major consumer electronics companies face significant supply chain and product availability risks from ITC exclusion orders, particularly when integrating third-party patented health technologies into mass-market devices.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB correctly construed the claim term 'encryption information' in a patent covering systems for streaming partly encrypted media content, which affected the obviousness determination.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the PTAB's claim construction of 'encryption information' in DivX's streaming media patent, vacated the Board's decision rejecting Netflix's obviousness challenge, and remanded for further proceedings. The ruling could render the patent's claims unpatentable over prior art under the corrected construction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Streaming and media technology companies benefit from a narrowing claim construction that may invalidate patents covering common encrypted streaming techniques, reducing licensing exposure.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the digital media streaming space face increased vulnerability to IPR challenges when claim terms are given broader-than-warranted constructions that distinguish over prior art.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment regardless of personal knowledge, and whether source code constitutes hearsay, in the context of proving the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) corporate representative testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge of the events, and that computer source code is not hearsay because code commands are not 'statements.' The ruling facilitated proof that a prior art device was commercially sold before the patent's critical date.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from expanded evidentiary tools to prove on-sale bar invalidity, as corporate representative testimony and source code evidence are more readily admissible even when original witnesses are unavailable.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased invalidity risk from the on-sale bar, as defendants can rely on 30(b)(6) testimony from current employees who lack personal knowledge and on source code evidence to prove prior commercial sales.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled declaratory judgment action when it previously missed the deadline for seeking a stay of an earlier-filed action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for mandatory stays by dismissing and refiling a declaratory judgment action. The court ruled that BioMarin could not obtain a mandatory stay of Ascendis's refiled DJ action after having missed the 30-day deadline in the original action, preventing gamesmanship with parallel ITC and district court proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent challengers benefit from protection against litigation delay tactics, as ITC respondents cannot manipulate filing deadlines to freeze district court proceedings through strategic dismissal and refiling of declaratory judgment actions.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents who miss the 30-day mandatory stay deadline lose this procedural tool permanently for the same dispute, even if they refile the district court action, requiring more careful attention to statutory deadlines.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTO Director's instructions to the PTAB governing discretionary denials of inter partes review institution constitute 'general statements of policy' exempt from APA notice-and-comment rulemaking under 5 U.S.C. § 553(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the PTO Director's instructions governing discretionary IPR institution decisions are general statements of policy exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking. The court held that because Congress gave the Director unreviewable discretion over institution and the instructions do not bind the Director, they need not go through formal rulemaking procedures.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the PTO Director's preserved flexibility to issue and modify discretionary denial policies without formal rulemaking, which has historically led to denials that protect patent rights from duplicative challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to challenge patents through IPR face continued uncertainty from non-institution policies that can change without public input, limiting their ability to rely on IPR as a consistent tool for patent validity challenges.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER operations, and whether the incentive awards to class representatives were proper.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal courts exceeded statutory authority by charging PACER fees to fund non-PACER expenses. The court upheld attorneys' fees, costs, and incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives, noting that hundreds of thousands of PACER users will be fully or substantially reimbursed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses and law firms that are heavy PACER users benefit from substantial fee reimbursements covering an eight-year class period, and the settlement establishes a precedent limiting the government's ability to cross-subsidize unrelated systems with user fees.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that four asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether generally known information in a field can constitute trade secrets or inventive contributions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's trade secret misappropriation verdict, holding that the plaintiff failed to prove the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known in the field. The court also reversed patent invalidity findings and vacated the permanent injunction and exemplary damages, while affirming counterfeiting liability for unauthorized trademark use.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from heightened scrutiny of whether asserted trade secrets are truly protectable, particularly where the information is generally known in the relevant field.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection face increased difficulty sustaining misappropriation claims when the underlying knowledge overlaps with information generally known in the industry, even if specific compilations are proprietary.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence where dependent claims recited a 'predetermined time delay' for restricting access to sensor information, and whether a non-party to district court litigation could file IPR petitions challenging patents asserted in that litigation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination regarding FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent claims, finding insufficient evidence to support the Board's conclusion that prior art disclosed the claimed 'predetermined time delay' feature. The ruling addresses the growing concern of third-party IPR petitions filed on behalf of or in coordination with actual litigants to circumvent the one-year statutory time bar.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from closer scrutiny of IPR obviousness findings and potential limits on third-party petitioners who may be acting as proxies for time-barred parties in related litigation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to use IPR as a defensive tool face increased risk that the Board's invalidity findings will be vacated on appeal for insufficient evidence, particularly on specific claim limitations.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a patent damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy where the expert used a comparable-license methodology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report in a patent case against Microsoft involving Azure cloud networking technology, and vacated the resulting summary judgment for absence of a remedy. The ruling reinforces that comparable-license methodologies for patent damages should not be excluded merely because of disagreements about the comparability of selected licenses.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from a more permissive standard for admitting damages expert testimony based on comparable licenses, reducing the risk that cases will be dismissed on summary judgment for lack of a quantifiable remedy.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies defending against patent claims face greater difficulty in excluding damages evidence at the Daubert stage, potentially increasing settlement pressure even where damages theories are contested.
